    #65281. Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1486 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1486 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, from left, Sens.
    • The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.
    • It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, from left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

    It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

    The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

    Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

    However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

    The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

    It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new authority over interstate transmission lines.

    It also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

    Democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately said they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

    The "massive four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

    "This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito noted before passage.

    In a recent development, ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

    It has been revealed that wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

    The Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

    That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

    The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

    The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

    None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

    The bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, plan and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

    The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

    The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

    Industry observers note that speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., stated last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

    Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member New Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as right now drafted.

    However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an glitch: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

    And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the upcoming Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

    Recent findings suggest that merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both said the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

    According to recent reports, some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

    "I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley mentioned before the vote Thursday night.

    In a recent development, but Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental complications under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

    While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

    As part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

    However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

    In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

    Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

    Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

    Sources indicate that after decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

    According to recent reports, lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the headliners of this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, a ruling of state-sponsored genocide in Myanmar, and Anthropic’s record-setting public debut.

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the headliners of this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, a ruling of state-sponsored genocide in Myanmar, and Anthropic’s record-setting public debut.

    A week of high-level diplomacy capped off on Thursday with a trilateral summit featuring U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin. But although the meeting, which took place at a sprawling lakeside villa in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, was initially framed as an opportunity to pursue global peacemaking, analysts noted it proved to be little more than a photo op.

    According to recent reports, heading into the dialogue, Trump was clear about what he hoped to accomplish. “The United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used,” the U.S. president said at the start of the summit. The three countries hold more than 90 percent of the world’s total nuclear weapons.

    According to recent reports, yet the roughly 70-minute meeting concluded with no mention of future nuclear negotiations or a potential arms reduction treaty. Instead, the three leaders released a peace declaration that “reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” It was one of just four items listed in the joint statement—and the last one mentioned.

    No. 1 on the list was a commitment to reform the United Nations. The United States, China, and Russia are three of the five permanent members on the U.N. Security Council, granting them significant sway over the international body’s actions. Yet all three nations have repeatedly accused the U.N. of bias.

    The second item noted the three leaders “proposal to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations” and “reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows.” It did not specify how much additional crude would be provided to help stabilize the market, though the United States has already made efforts to suspend sanctions on Russian oil—to the condemnation of Washington’s Western allies—to ease economic pressures.

    Item three concerned the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar bodies, with the three leaders arguing that these courts “must not abuse their jurisdiction,” particularly against state officials who they claim have immunity.

    In a recent development, the Trump administration has sought to dismantle the ICC by questioning its status and imposing sanctions on its members; the court is a “rogue globalist organization,” Trump said on Thursday. Putin has similarly denounced the ICC’s authority, particularly after it issued an arrest warrant for him in 2023 citing alleged war crimes. Moscow denies the accusations.

    According to recent reports, the trio walked away from Thursday’s meeting with optimistic outlooks. Trump characterized the summit as a “Great and Highly Consequential Trip”; Xi described the talks as “positive, constructive, and fruitful”; and Putin said they were “open and candid.”.

    However, not everyone shared those sentiments. “It’s a historic embarrassment that people will remember long into the future,” U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer stated on Thursday. “It’s a betrayal of the United States by a president who loves nothing more than to bow down to our adversaries for a photo op.”.

    According to recent reports, guilty of genocide. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on Thursday that Myanmar had committed genocide against the country’s minority Rohingya Muslim community beginning in August 2017. This is the first time that the highest U.N. court has found a nation directly responsible for genocide.

    Sources indicate that “The court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said in the 9-6 ruling. The 15-judge panel, which included 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay, rejected the country’s defense that its so-called “clearance operations” were a legitimate campaign against insurgents.

    Although the ICJ does not have an enforcement mechanism, the landmark decision could help determine future reparations for Rohingya survivors as well as prevent the current junta-led state from casting off its diplomatic pariah status; Myanmar’s military regime has recently tried to rebrand itself as a nominally civilian government.

    The case, filed by Gambia in 2019, could also impact how the world’s top court handles similar genocide allegations linked to the wars in Gaza and Ukraine. Thursday’s judgment is “a demonstration of international justice & a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand,” U.N. chief António Guterres wrote on X.

    Record IPO. Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday, and already, interest has exceeded expectations. In its initial public offering on Wednesday, the U.S.-based company behind the artificial intelligence chatbot Claude sold 980 million shares for $83 a pop, raising $83.1 billion. Such a blockbuster showing put Anthropic above SpaceX, the previous debut record-holder, to become the largest stock market opener in history.

    On Thursday, the AI organization began trading shares for the first time. It opened at $111.50 per share, pushing Anthropic’s market value to roughly $2 trillion.

    Since Anthropic was founded in 2021, global interest in AI has skyrocketed, with the United States and China leading the charge. Trump has characterized its advancement as akin to the Industrial Revolution, and Xi has similarly invested tens of billions of dollars in its development. AI has become a growing component of modern warfare, driven global markets, and raised security and environmental concerns.

    According to recent reports, but as AI has become more powerful, some have begun to warn that the world should pull back. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei led calls in September to place guardrails on the tech’s advancement after former Anthropic employees warned of security risks. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote at the time. “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems.”.

    Sources indicate that trump’s Greenland win. Danish lawmakers unanimously approved a security deal on Thursday that will allow the United States to strengthen its presence in Greenland and the wider Arctic region. The deal, which expands on a 1951 defense agreement between the United States and Denmark, aims to defuse months of tensions over the Trump administration’s repeated threats to seize the semiautonomous, mineral-rich territory of Greenland.

    “We have been through a difficult time, during which many people here at home have been concerned about our country and our future,” Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen wrote on Facebook on Thursday. “I hope that today’s decision will help bring greater calm and a sense of security.”.

    First announced in September, the latest deal will allow the U.S. military to construct more bases on Greenland, “modernize and expand” its activities at Pituffik Space Base, and set up “defense areas” to bolster its Golden Dome ambitions. In exchange, the territory will remain under Danish control, and Greenland will respect its commitments to the United States if it chooses to seek independence.

    One of the most anticipated video game releases is finally here. Grand Theft Auto VI rolled out at midnight on Thursday, starting in Newly introduced Zealand and moving across time zones from Tokyo to London before finally reaching Miami—the inspiration for the game’s Vice City. More than 19 million copies of the open-world action-adventure game have already been sold, amounting to roughly $1.84 billion. Experts anticipate the game’s nearly 100 missions—in which players inhabit the world of a Bonnie and Clyde-like crime duo—to take around 50 hours to complete, so don’t be concerned if you don’t hear from your gamer friends over the next few days.

    #65278. Why Israel Is Losing America

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2373 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Israel Is Losing America

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress.
    • Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Crucial Ally.
    • According to recent reports, american politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Issues on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

    Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Crucial Ally.

    According to recent reports, american politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

    As I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

    Things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a new paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

    Sources indicate that this change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

    It has been revealed that whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a new U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

    Trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

    Time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace blueprint for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is at the moment marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

    Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he said himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

    Trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

    Trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

    Unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising newly introduced ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

    Israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, announced wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

    Industry observers note that israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

    According to recent reports, without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

    Sources indicate that it is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

    Israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with new realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s plan for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

    Israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

    Israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of upcoming Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

    Israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

    In a recent development, these steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

    If Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

    Millions could lose paid benefits due to Congress ignoring decades of Social Security warnings: experts

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, and Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, warned that Congress’ 50 years of action have led Social Security to the cliff of insolvency.
    • A panel filled with top economists, including a Nobel Peace Prize winner, warned Congress decades ago that its reforms to Social Security could spell disaster.
    • Now, experts tell Fox News Digital that the group from a bygone era was right as the safety net program hurtles toward a crisis that could affect millions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, and Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, warned that Congress’ 50 years of action have led Social Security to the cliff of insolvency.

    A panel filled with top economists, including a Nobel Peace Prize winner, warned Congress decades ago that its reforms to Social Security could spell disaster.

    Now, experts tell Fox News Digital that the group from a bygone era was right as the safety net program hurtles toward a crisis that could affect millions.

    "Social Security benefits were put on autopilot back in 1977," Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow of the American Enterprise Institute, told Fox News Digital. "Since then, Congress has done as little as it possibly could.".

    Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., unveiled a report on the decades-old program that blasted it as a "Ponzi scheme" and warned that Social Security’s slide into insolvency began in the 1970s, when, despite warnings, lawmakers opted to tie benefit growth to wages rather than inflation.

    AMERICANS MISLED ON SOCIAL SECURITY FOR DECADES AS CLOCK COUNTS DOWN ON BENEFITS, EXPLOSIVE REPORT REVEALS.

    Recent findings suggest that president Jimmy Carter shakes hands with Louisiana Sen. Russell Long after signing the Social Security bill at the White House in Washington on Dec. 20, 1977. (Getty Archive).

    Johnson wrote in his report that, at the time, an expert panel was formed that warned lawmakers that if they were to tie benefits to inflation, "Social Security would likely be sustainable today.".

    Still, lawmakers at the time ran with their own amendments to the program, which were signed into law by former President Jimmy Carter in December 1977.

    "What they said in 1977 was if you index benefit growth to wages, you're effectively building a solvency crisis into the program," Biggs said. "You are over-promising, you're going to build in benefits that the current system can't afford to pay and you're committing future taxpayers to pay rates of taxes that the taxpayers in 1977 weren't willing to pay.".

    In the decades since, Congress has done little to change the program.

    SENATE REPUBLICANS BREAK THROUGH WASHINGTON GRIDLOCK WITH MASSIVE AMERICAN ENERGY, DATA CENTER OVERHAUL.

    Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, told Fox News Digital that’s largely because lawmakers have not had the political will to do it.

    She agreed with Johnson that Social Security was effectively a "Ponzi scheme," and stated "there's this misconception that a lot of Americans think that Social Security is a retirement savings program.".

    "But for that, you would actually need to have savings occur in the system, and there would need to be assets that would be invested in earning returns," Boccia mentioned. "That's not the case. We're talking about a pay-as-you-go program.".

    One of the side effects of Congress’ lack of action to rein in the program is that the wage growth formula relies on workers in the economy contributing with their paychecks.

    Boccia noted that as the decades have gone on, "we've seen a severe decline in the number of workers compared to the number of retirees collecting benefits as a result of a decline in fertility.".

    DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN.

    It has been revealed that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., makes his way to votes in the U.S. Capitol Sept. 30, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images).

    Congress’ last real successful effort to reform Social Security came in the early 1980s, Biggs noted, when lawmakers were forced to step in to deal with the "funding crisis" hitting the program.

    Sources indicate that "They raised taxes. They increased the retirement age. So, they did this with months to spare to fix Social Security," Biggs said. "It's not something they wanted to do, but they were forced to do.

    "Now, in 2032, we're going to face the same situation, where Congress will be forced to take action sometime before the trust fund runs out in 2032, not because they want to, but because they're forced to do it," he continued.

    If Social Security’s trust fund runs dry by 2032, Americans’ benefits would be slashed, and the onus of paying for the shortfall would add trillions more to the nation’s debt.

    But Johnson, in his report, declared that the Social Security problem could not be fixed between now and then because of Congress’ inaction for the last several decades. And he suggested the solution would be to repeal a possible benefits reduction as the program’s trust fund heads toward insolvency in just under seven years.

    Industry observers note that biggs, who was part of former President George W. Bush’s effort to reform Social Security over two decades ago, said that, had Congress taken action "25 years ago, you could fix Social Security in barely noticeable ways.".

    "There is no easy fix to Social Security today, and that stems entirely from the fact that, every year, when Congress has had the opportunity to fix Social Security, they chose to duck the concern for political reasons and kick the can down the road," Biggs said.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    Boccia disagreed with Johnson’s solution and contended that the real answer was one that lawmakers of yesterday and today would be hesitant to approach — raising taxes.

    "The real way to think about this is that there's almost no way to imagine Congress would let those benefit cuts take effect," Boccia noted. "It will be so politically toxic. So, most likely they're going to try to find a different solution.

    "The last time the trust fund was running out of money in 1982, Congress put together a commission and then voted on a bill that increased taxes and reduced benefits, including raising the social security retirement age," she continued.

    "The problem is that the funding gap now is much larger, more than two times bigger than it was in the ‘80s.".

    In a recent development, alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

    The Iran war appears to be heating up (again), as diplomatic talks have hit a wall (again). The United States and Iran resumed strikes over the past week, ending a roughly two-month lull in the conflict.

    The renewed fighting has come as Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and amid an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports.

    Tit-for-tat. Over the past six days, Iran released a series of strikes on U.S. assets in Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, and an air base in Kuwait that hosts U.S. forces.

    Sources indicate that iran targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in Bahrain on Friday and took aim at a radar system at a helicopter base in the tiny island nation on Sunday. No damage was reported. Tehran mentioned the attacks were in retaliation for U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers as well as ongoing drone surveillance operations.

    On Tuesday, Iran targeted another radar facility in Bahrain with drones, which were reportedly intercepted; the United States retaliated with a strike on an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island. Iran responded on Wednesday with an attack on Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait. There were no reports of damage. Bahrain also said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday.

    Recent findings suggest that under pressure. U.S. President Donald Trump has been vague about his plans in the war, and some reports suggest he is mulling over ordering expansive strikes. But Trump on Thursday indicated that he’s not in a hurry to escalate. “I am not rushing into any decision. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year,” Trump told Axios.

    Trump’s comments came as Israel is reportedly pressing the White House to escalate with a fresh bombing campaign. Roman Gofman, the director of the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad, visited Washington this week, where he is said to have expressed concerns to U.S. officials over alleged Iranian chemical weapons development.

    In a recent development, the United States also has intelligence that Iran has drawn up plans to potentially use a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington, according to a CNN report. Trump on Tuesday said the United States was looking into the dirty bomb report and takes it “very seriously.” But he later downplayed the prospect of Iran actually using such a weapon in Washington, and he warned that “if it does happen, we’ll wipe them out.” Trump this week also told Fox News there’s “indication that Iran is looking at gasses, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “And they’re looking at gas and biological weapons. Not nice. And we’ll see,” he said.

    Expired. If Trump does decide to ramp up the war, experts have warned that it would be a huge gamble and would undoubtedly lead to further retaliatory attacks on U.S. forces and assets in the region. The U.S. intelligence community reportedly assesses that Iran has a stockpile of up to 2,500 missiles in its arsenal, despite prior claims from the Trump administration of such capabilities being destroyed. Iran also remains defiant in the face of continued U.S. economic pressure, and Tehran appears emboldened by major Republican losses in the midterm elections.

    The United States still has significant military assets in the region, including two aircraft carriers (after yet another reshuffling that saw the USS George Washington leave the Middle East this week, following the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt). But the United States is also facing significant constraints, and the war has depleted stockpiles of key munitions. Due to such shortages, acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao this week told senators that U.S. forces resorted to firing expired munitions in the war.

Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang came back, and Huang himself fueled the fire with a lengthy post on X in which he wrote: “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

    Tech Report: Departing Senate spending kingpins angle for last earmark hurrah

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., won't be smiling as much if Democrats force a punt on spending bills to next year.
    • Newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec.
    • Nearly 4,000 individual earmarks are contained in nine of the 12 draft fiscal 2027 spending bills, a CQ Roll Call tally found; the remaining three bills — Defense, State-Foreign Operations and Legislative Branch — don't have any.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., won't be smiling as much if Democrats force a punt on spending bills to next year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

    Newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    Nearly 4,000 individual earmarks are contained in nine of the 12 draft fiscal 2027 spending bills, a CQ Roll Call tally found; the remaining three bills — Defense, State-Foreign Operations and Legislative Branch — don't have any.

    In a recent development, there's typically some overlap between House and Senate projects that would get weeded out in final negotiations to avoid duplication. But for comparison's sake, House Republicans included nearly 6,700 line items worth $8.2 billion in their earmarked spending bills.

    Democrats have signaled they'll push for a continuing resolution into the first quarter of next year enabling them to rewrite the full-year fiscal 2027 bills when they take the gavels in January, possibly upping the overall pot of earmarked funds — or at least divvying up the pie more favorably to blue states and districts.

    But that would mean the final attempt by departing lawmakers like Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and longtime Senate GOP leader and senior appropriator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, to deliver for their states might be all for naught.

    And top Democrats with substantial earmarking success under GOP governance, such as Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., will have to start from scratch.

    Here are some key stats on senators' earmarks in the latest batch of spending bills Collins is trying to get across the finish line.

    Naturally, much of the spoils go to Senate Appropriations Committee members, and that's no different this year. But with so many more Democrats requesting projects — often jointly with their fellow delegation member — individual contributions may appear diluted given they have to share the credit.

    That dilution shows up in the rankings when allocating credit in a way that avoids double-counting — everyone gets an equal share of his or her joint projects, so $20 million sponsored jointly by two senators will appear as $10 million for each. Solo earmarkers in this scenario face no such dilution.

    Using the even-split methodology, the top 10 — all senior appropriators — look like this:.

    Another way to look at it is by simply adding up every instance of a senator affixing his or her name to a project, which leads to double-counting but gives them full credit for every earmark secured, even with jointly requested projects.

    Here's the top 10 in that scenario:.

    Finally, there's the solo earmarker leaderboard, only counting dollars secured without any co-sponsors:.

    McConnell and Collins hit the trifecta, ending up among the top three in all three scenarios.

    Related: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks.

    Unlike the House, where states with the largest populations receive the most funding by virtue of having more representatives securing earmarks, smaller states punch above their weight in the Senate — particularly when their delegations achieve exalted positions of seniority.

    Hence Washington state — with Murray and Cantwell, the Commerce Committee ranking member, representing it — is way out in front.

    By contrast, the second- and third-most populous states — Texas and Florida — received a grand total of zero earmarked funds, because their GOP senators didn't request any. California, with the largest population, is No. 16 in the ranks; Newly introduced York is 12th.

    Here are the top 10 states by earmarked funds procured in the Senate bills, clearly skewing toward smaller, typically reddish states:.

    The Transportation-HUD spending bill continues to be the go-to place for earmarks, accounting for 27 percent of all individual projects in the Senate bills and about one-third of all the earmarked dollars. The next-closest bill, Labor-HHS-Education, has half the earmarked amount that the "T-HUD" bill does.

    Top agencies and programs with earmarked funds are housed within, that's right, the departments of Transportation and Housing and Urban Development, with HUD leading the pack thanks to its ever-popular Community Development Fund accounting for all of that department's earmarks.

    In a recent development, transportation isn't far behind, thanks largely to highway projects, followed by Health and Human Services and its Health Resources and Services Administration account, which funds community health centers. Defense Department military construction projects and the Army Corps of Engineers round out the group of $1 billion-plus agencies.

    Here are the top accounts for earmarked funds in this year's crop of bills:.

    The biggest individual earmarks are largely within Army Corps accounts funded in the draft Energy-Water bill, with some military construction and transportation projects and two mega NIST-based university construction earmarks thrown in on behalf of Collins and McConnell.

    #65271. Three Routes to VPP Revenue for Installers, EPCs, and Developers Utility programs, wholesale markets, and bilateral contracts each come with different eligibility rules, payment structures, and commercial responsibilities.

    Three Routes to VPP Revenue for Installers, EPCs, and Developers Utility programs, wholesale markets, and bilateral contracts each come with different eligibility rules, payment structures, and commercial responsibilities.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, in June 2026, Google and Voltus announced a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM.
    • The deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs.
    • Industry observers note that utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

    According to recent reports, in June 2026, Google and Voltus announced a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

    The deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

    Utility programs and procurement.

    Industry observers note that utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

    Sources indicate that beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

    It has been revealed that aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

    While Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. Upcoming York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

    Wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

    Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

    Bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

    The appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

    #65268. The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2266 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.
    • Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested.
    • Recent findings suggest that turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.

    Ankara’s Risky Bid to Impose Regional Order.

    Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested. The previous Gulf-centered order had Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) trying to stabilize and shape the region using economic statecraft and the normalization of relations with former foes in Iran, Israel, Turkey, and Syria. Three years of war in Gaza, and more recently in Iran and the Gulf, have severely disrupted that order-building project and generated a deep sense of uncertainty about what comes next.

    Recent findings suggest that turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum. Before 2023, Ankara’s influence had been in decline; after years of diplomatic isolation following the Arab uprisings, it had just begun repairing its ties with major regional actors. But in the past few years, Turkey has earned American backing for its policies in Syria and its regional diplomacy, and it has made an effort to secure the home front by pursuing a peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a militant group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the Turkish state. Most recently, in August, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey signed the Mecca Defense Alliance, a collective security agreement that institutionalizes Turkey’s regional positioning and pulls the country directly into Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis.

    Turkey’s post–October 7 strategy has restored the country’s position as a regional heavyweight. But it is not capable of meeting its larger objective: establishing order on its own terms. Turkey, like the region’s other aspiring leaders, lacks the power to impose a latest security framework on its own. Its nascent efforts to build one, such as the new Mecca pact, merely make countries outside the bloc feel unsafe, feeding instability. Turkey’s most ambitious plays for regional leadership are therefore likely to prove ineffective or even counterproductive. As long as the Middle East’s highly militarized, zero-sum security dynamics remain, Ankara would be better off concentrating on interests closer to home that it has the power to protect.

    This is not the first time that Turkey has tried to shape the broader Middle Eastern order. Ankara saw the Arab uprisings in the early 2010s as a historic window of opportunity. The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) described the political transformation sweeping the region as “the people’s coming to power,” and the Turkish government expected that eventual elections in the Arab countries rocked by protest would bring into office parties aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood, which was ideologically sympathetic and had practical links to the AKP. The emergence of friendly governments, the thinking went, would increase Turkey’s influence in the region.

    Yet these hopes soon receded. Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood–affiliated president, Mohamed Morsi, was overthrown in 2013, and Turkey’s bet on the opposition movement in Syria failed as Bashar al-Assad clung to power. Turkey was left isolated. A rival axis composed of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE objected to Turkey’s Muslim Brotherhood ties and sought to limit Ankara’s influence. This group contested Turkey’s positions across the Middle East, North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Horn of Africa, effectively fighting proxy battles with Turkey in conflicts in Libya, Somalia, and Syria.

    Then, the attacks on October 7, 2023, ushered in another period of upheaval. Some changes since have played in Turkey’s favor. Chief among them is the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024 at the hands of opposition groups led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. Turkey had arguably invested more than any other country in pursuit of regime change in Damascus; it assisted opposition groups for years. Yet as the years went by, that objective seemed increasingly out of reach. The region’s other major powers made their peace with the regime’s survival, and even Ankara began considering rapprochement with Assad to avoid being left out in the cold. Assad’s fall changed Turkey’s fortunes overnight, handing it a level of influence in Syria it had not held in more than a decade.

    Sources indicate that other developments proved more dangerous for Ankara. Israel’s foreign policy became more assertive and revisionist after October 7, and its expansive security objectives began to clash with Turkey’s own. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s sharp criticism of Israeli policies in Gaza strained the relationship, and it deteriorated further when Turkey expanded its foothold in post-Assad Syria and Israel came to view Ankara’s military presence there as a direct threat. As Israel continues to strike sites in Syria—attacks Ankara has condemned—the risk of escalation is only growing. A miscalculation on either side could lead to a direct clash between Israeli and Turkish forces.

    In a recent development, the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, meanwhile, has cut both ways for Turkey. While Tehran’s attention has been focused elsewhere, Ankara has welcomed Iran’s retreat from Syria and the chance to push back against its remaining influence in Iraq. Turkey also has no interest in seeing a nuclear-armed Iran upend the regional balance of power. Yet the prospect of chaos across Turkey’s eastern border, should the Iranian regime fall, has bred real anxiety in Ankara, as has the possibility that Iran could become emboldened if the regime emerges from the war intact.

    In this complex environment, Ankara has pursued a three-pronged strategy to protect its security interests and, it hopes, capitalize on opportunities the upheaval has created. Since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to power, Erdogan has drawn Turkey closer to the United States and tried to use his relationship with Washington to advance Ankara’s regional policies. Turkey has also pressed ahead with regional normalization, building on efforts to repair ties with Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other key Arab countries in the early 2020s, with the aim to forge a broader regional bloc. And, domestically, Ankara introduced the “Turkey Without Terror” process, an attempt to resolve the conflict with the PKK inside and outside Turkey, which Turkey’s adversaries have long exploited by arming Kurdish groups or backing them politically.

    Industry observers note that some of Ankara’s policies have borne fruit. Consider, for instance, the outreach to Washington. Erdogan’s close relations with Trump helped bring the United States on board with Turkey’s expanded role in Syria. Turkey was one of the four countries Washington brought in to help negotiate the U.S.-proposed October 2025 cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas, and as a result, Trump offered and Erdogan accepted a seat on the U.S. president’s so-called Board of Peace for Gaza’s reconstruction. Turkey has played an active part mediating between the United States and Iran during the latest war. And Trump publicly endorsed the Mecca Defense Alliance, calling it “big, bold, and key.” All of this points to a recognition in Washington of Turkey’s regional importance, the U.S. administration’s willingness to support some of Ankara’s priorities, and Turkey’s determination to elevate its own position.

    It has been revealed that yet there are undeniable limits to Turkey’s quest for influence. At a February 2026 Board of Peace summit, for instance, Turkey was excluded from participating in a planned international troop deployment and police training in Gaza—a sign that warming relations with Washington were not enough to override Israeli objections to having a Turkish military footprint in the Palestinian territory. In Syria, similarly, the support Turkey has secured from the Trump administration has not stopped Israel from launching military strikes at Syrian targets near Turkish positions. Simply put, Turkey has not been able to use its relationship with the Trump administration to overcome the limit Israeli opposition places on the scope of Turkey’s regional role.

    According to recent reports, turkey’s regional normalization efforts have yielded mixed results, too. Restoring diplomatic ties with significant players such as Saudi Arabia is in Turkey’s interest, to be sure. But the alliances Ankara is entering with these countries risk making Turkey and the region less secure, not more. The Mecca pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia could end up hardening rival blocs and elevating regional tensions. Turkey insists that the alliance is directed against no country in particular and has suggested that Egypt, Syria, or even Iran could eventually join. But in the meantime, Iran, Israel, and the Houthis could see it as a threat and try to test or weaken its members’ commitment.

    According to recent reports, furthermore, the pact could pull Turkey into other countries’ wars. That possibility is already on the table now that the Turkish parliament has ratified the agreement and the Houthis are escalating their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Turkish government has insisted that any military support it provided would be confined to deterrence, intelligence sharing, and defense-industrial cooperation. Yet Saudi Arabia is now seeking Pakistan’s and Turkey’s help with air defense and territorial protection, and the three states have agreed to prepare forces for rapid deployment. Sending Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia would still require separate parliamentary approval. If parliament allowed it, even a limited deployment would risk drawing Turkey into a wider regional conflict.

    Some kind of regional security framework is necessary. The problem is that no country in the region, including Turkey, has the power to impose a security order on the rest, so whenever someone tries, other countries feel threatened. An informal cooperation framework that is open to all countries in the region—and that asks its members to commit to nonaggression instead of making mutual-defense pledges—might work better. But the assembly and functioning of such a coalition require trust that governments in the region do not have. Breaking the impasse would likely require the United States to play a more constructive role than it has in recent years—not simply endorsing whatever regional arrangement emerges, as Trump did with the Mecca pact, or pressuring countries to normalize relations with Israel without expecting Israel to change its policies in return, as Trump has also done. Instead, Washington, perhaps with the help of Beijing, would need to compel regional rivals such as Iran and Saudi Arabia to take confidence-building measures that would make an inclusive security framework viable in the long run. Without this external push, the narrower security blocs that emerge in the region will only lead to further instability.

    Ankara’s strongest cards lie closer to home. The Kurdish peace process has moved slowly since February 2025, when Abdullah Ocalan, the imprisoned leader of the PKK, called on the militant group to disarm. But it has yielded tangible progress. In May 2025, the PKK announced that it would dissolve. In Syria, Kurdish forces are being integrated into the Syrian army, and Mazloum Abdi, the commander of the People’s Defense Units, a Kurdish armed group affiliated with the PKK, was appointed as a presidential adviser in August. Syria’s postconflict transition remains fragile, and the reconciliation between Damascus and Kurdish militants in the northeast may owe as much to American pressure as it does to Turkey’s domestic efforts to make peace with the PKK. But for Turkey, the eventual integration of Syrian Kurdish forces into the Syrian state removes the risk Ankara saw in having an autonomous, armed Kurdish entity on its southern border. And, given the close security and economic ties Ankara has developed with Damascus, as well as the political and legal steps the government can take at home to complete the disbanding of the PKK and to deepen democratic reforms, Turkey has the ability to keep these encouraging developments on track.

    Sources indicate that turkey’s regional policies are most successful when the country plays to its strengths—not when it is trying to throw its weight around the region. In the first decade of the twenty-first century, Ankara built real influence by mediating between Syria and Israel and between Palestinian factions, expanding its economic engagement in the Levant, and proposing projects to connect the region’s energy and transportation infrastructure. Military power, meanwhile, has proved most effective when applied for specific purposes, such as to secure the border with Syria. This combination is Turkey’s winning formula: diplomacy and economic outreach to extend its influence, and limited force to protect its core interests. Broad, open-ended commitments, by contrast, risk drawing Turkey into regional conflicts without making it safer.

    Today, sticking to a more effective formula does not mean retreating from regional politics. It means setting priorities and planning long-term. Consolidating the Kurdish peace process, keeping Washington invested in Syria’s stabilization, managing the risk of confrontation with Israel in Syria, and maintaining constructive relations with the Kurdistan Regional Government in northern Iraq and the Iraqi government in Baghdad are key to keeping Turkey’s borders secure and are within Turkey’s ability to achieve. Ankara can continue to use its experience in mediation when opportunities to advance peace processes present themselves. It can also promote economic connectivity, both by expanding trade ties and by supporting regional infrastructure projects such as the Iraq-Europe Development Road and a proposed pipeline network connecting the Gulf to Jordan, Syria, and Turkey. It need not shy away from security cooperation with the Gulf, either, if it can engage without making formal commitments. Yet in all these endeavors, Ankara should remember that it has the most clout when it stays out of the region’s conflicts.

    In a recent development, the Middle East’s escalating wars and rival blocs could make a narrower Turkish security policy more difficult to sustain today than it was in the past. Defending Ankara’s interests and playing a constructive role in a volatile neighborhood will require a careful balance. The best way Turkey can contribute to regional stability may be to avoid trying to do too much.

    Breaking: The Other Summitry in Shenzhen
